title: President & Vice-President
summary: How the President and Vice-President are elected and removed, and what powers they have.

subcards.title: President: election & office (Art 52–62)
subcards.summary: How the President is elected, who can stand, and the conditions of office.
at_a_glance: Art 52–62 (office, election, term, oath); Art 71 (election disputes); Art 361 (immunities)
Elected MPs and elected MLAs of all States, Delhi and Puducherry
Proportional representation by single transferable vote; secret ballot

blocks.text: Part V of the Constitution (Articles 52 to 78) deals with the Union executive (the people who run the Central Government): the President, the Vice-President, the Prime Minister, the Council of Ministers and the Attorney General of India. The President is the head of the Indian State and the first citizen of India.

blocks.title: Articles on the President's office
head: Article
What it says
rows: There shall be a President of India (creates the office)
The executive power of the Union is vested in (given to) the President. Art 53(3)(b): Parliament may, by law, give functions to authorities other than the President
Election of the President (who forms the electoral college)
Manner of election (value of votes, proportional representation by single transferable vote, secret ballot)
Term of office is 5 years. The President resigns by writing to the Vice-President, and continues in office until the successor takes charge
Conditions of the President's office (not a legislator, no office of profit, rent-free residence, emoluments)
Oath or affirmation, administered by the Chief Justice of India
Time of holding election to fill a vacancy
Disputes about the election of the President or Vice-President are decided by the Supreme Court
Immunities (legal protection) of the President and Governors
Appointment of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers
Appointment of the Governor of a State by the President
Appointment of the Chief Minister and the State Council of Ministers

blocks.title: Linked facts
items: Art 59(1): the President shall not be a member of either House of Parliament. Art 79: yet Parliament consists of the President and the two Houses (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Both are stated in the Constitution.
Entry to office: the President is elected (indirectly, through an electoral college); the Prime Minister and the Governor are appointed by the President.

Why indirect election? It suits the parliamentary system (the President is only a nominal (name-only) head) and a direct election by the whole country would be very costly. Election by Parliament alone was rejected so that the President represents both the Union and the States.

sections.heading: Electoral college: who votes and who does not

blocks.text: Electoral college = the special group of voters who elect the President (Art 54). The people do not vote directly.

blocks.title: Who takes part? (MP = Member of Parliament; MLA = Member of Legislative Assembly; MLC = Member of Legislative Council)
head: Category
Elects President
Elects Vice-President
Impeaches President
rows: Elected MPs (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha)
Elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry
Yes, added by the 70th Amendment (1992), in force from 1 June 1995
Nominated MLAs (e.g. nominated members of Puducherry Assembly)
MLCs (members of State Legislative Councils), elected or nominated

items: A Chief Minister who is an MLC (member of the Legislative Council, not the Assembly) cannot vote in the presidential election.
If a State Assembly is dissolved, its members cannot vote, even if fresh elections are not held before the presidential election.
Delhi Assembly has no nominated members. The 104th Amendment (2019) ended nomination of Anglo-Indians to Lok Sabha and Assemblies (from 25 January 2020).

Jammu and Kashmir: Art 54 names only Delhi and Puducherry. J&K had no Assembly in 2022, so it did not vote. Whether the MLAs of the new Union Territory of J&K (Assembly elected 2024) can vote is not clearly settled by Art 54 or the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 (as of Nov 2026).
A nominated MP can vote in the Vice-Presidential election but not in the Presidential election. The Constitution does not stop a nominated member from becoming a Union minister.

sections.heading: Value of votes and counting (with worked example)

blocks.text: Art 55 aims at two things. (a) Uniformity among States: each MLA's vote value reflects the population he or she represents. (b) Parity (equality) between the States and the Union: the total vote value of all MPs is about equal to the total vote value of all MLAs.

blocks.title: The two formulas
head: Voter
Value of one vote
rows: Divide the State's population by its number of elected MLAs, then divide by 1000. If the remainder is 500 or more, add 1.
Add up the vote values of all MLAs of all States (including Delhi and Puducherry), then divide by the total number of elected MPs. A fraction above one-half counts as 1.
blocks.note: Population means the 1971 census figures, until the figures of the first census taken after 2026 are published (84th Amendment, 2001). This 'freeze' ensures States that controlled their population do not lose vote value.

blocks.title: Worked example: Andhra Pradesh MLA (2022 figures)

steps.step: Population of AP (1971 census) = 2,78,00,586; elected MLAs = 175

steps.detail: 860 is 500 or more, so add 1

steps.step: Value of one AP MLA vote = 159
steps.detail: Total for AP = 159 × 175 = 27,825

blocks.title: Worked example: value of an MP vote (2022)

steps.step: Total value of all MLAs' votes (4,033 MLAs) = 5,43,231
Elected MPs = 543 Lok Sabha + 233 Rajya Sabha = 776

steps.detail: Total MP value = 700 × 776 = 5,43,200

blocks.title: Value of one MLA vote (2022) — some States
head: State or Union Territory
Value
blocks.note: Value depends on population per seat, not on the number of seats. All MPs (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha) have the same value (700 in 2022).

blocks.title: Counting: proportional representation by single transferable vote, secret ballot

steps.step: Each elector gets one ballot and marks preferences 1, 2, 3 … (as many as there are candidates)

steps.detail: This means more than half of the valid votes (an absolute majority)

steps.step: Count first preferences; if a candidate reaches the quota, he/she wins
If no one reaches the quota, remove the candidate with the fewest votes and transfer his or her ballots to the candidates marked as second preference. Repeat until someone reaches the quota
steps.detail: Only 1969 (V.V. Giri) was decided on second-preference votes

items: Critics in the Constituent Assembly said 'proportional representation' is a misnomer (wrong name), because only one seat is filled; it is really a preferential (alternative) vote system. 'Single transferable vote' is also not exact, because each elector's vote carries many value-units, not one.

sections.heading: Nomination and election disputes (1952 Act, Art 71)

blocks.title: Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 (as amended in 1997)
head: Item
President
Vice-President
rows: Security deposit (in Reserve Bank of India)
Candidate gets less than one-sixth of the votes polled
blocks.note: The 1997 increase was made to keep out non-serious candidates.

blocks.title: Article 71 (applies to both President and Vice-President)
head: Clause
Rule
rows: All doubts and disputes about the election are inquired into and decided by the Supreme Court only; its decision is final (not High Courts, not the Election Commission)
If the election is declared void, acts done by that person before the Supreme Court's decision remain valid
Parliament may by law regulate matters connected with the election (hence the 1952 Act). Regulating an election and deciding its disputes are separate functions.
The election cannot be challenged on the ground that the electoral college was incomplete (that is, some of its seats were vacant)

items: A presidential election cannot be postponed just because some State Assemblies are dissolved and their elections are pending; the dissolved Assemblies simply do not vote.
The Constitution prescribes no time limit within which the President must give or withhold assent to a Bill (Art 111).

blocks.title: Qualifications (Art 58)
head: Condition
rows: Qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha

Must not hold an office of profit (a paid post) under the Union, a State, a local authority or other public authority. A sitting President, Vice-President, Governor, Union minister or State minister is NOT treated as holding an office of profit, so he or she can contest.

blocks.title: Oath (Art 60)
items: Administered by the Chief Justice of India; in his absence, the seniormost available Supreme Court judge.
President swears to faithfully execute the office, to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law, and to devote himself/herself to the service and well-being of the people of India.
Anyone acting as President takes a similar oath.

blocks.title: Who administers whose oath / what the oath stresses
head: Office
Oath by
Key words
rows: Preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law
Chief Justice of the State High Court
Preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law
Faithful discharge of duties, and a separate oath of secrecy
Faith and allegiance to the Constitution; uphold the Constitution and laws
Faith and allegiance; faithfully discharge the duty
Governor or person appointed by him
Faith and allegiance to the Constitution

blocks.title: Conditions of office (Art 59)
head: Condition
rows: Must not be a member of Parliament or of a State Legislature (Assembly or Council). If such a member is elected, his or her seat is treated as vacated on the date he or she enters office as President (the same rule applies to the Vice-President under Art 66)
Must not hold any other office of profit
Entitled to official residence (Rashtrapati Bhavan) without paying rent
Gets emoluments (salary), allowances and privileges fixed by Parliament (until Parliament fixes them, as given in the Second Schedule)
Emoluments and allowances cannot be reduced during the term (the same protection applies to a Governor, Art 158(4))

items.what: Salary raised from ₹50,000 to ₹1.5 lakh per month; pension of retired President raised from ₹3 lakh a year to 50% of salary per month
Finance Act 2018 (effective 1 January 2016) raised salary from ₹1.5 lakh to ₹5 lakh per month
items.detail: Amended the President's Emoluments and Pension Act, 1951

blocks.title: Immunities (Art 361) — same for Governors
head: Clause
Protection
rows: Not answerable to any court for using official powers and duties. But Parliament can examine the President's conduct during impeachment, and cases can still be filed against the Government of India or the State Government.
No criminal proceedings can be started or continued during the term (even for personal acts)
No arrest or imprisonment process during the term
Civil proceedings for personal acts can be filed during the term only after 2 months' written notice
blocks.note: The immunity protects only the person. It does not put every government action beyond judicial review (checking by courts).

blocks.title: Form of address
items: Formally 'His/Her Excellency'. In October 2012, President Pranab Mukherjee approved a new protocol: within India, 'His Excellency' is dropped and 'Hon'ble President' is used (in Hindi, 'Rashtrapati Mahoday'). 'Excellency' is kept only for dealings with foreign dignitaries.
Term: 5 years from the date of entering office (Art 56).
The President stays in office beyond 5 years until the successor takes charge, so there is no interregnum (gap in office). The Vice-President does not act as President in this case.

The election for an ending term must be completed before the term ends (Art 62(1)). If the office falls vacant by death, resignation, removal or otherwise, an election must be held within 6 months, and the new President gets a full 5-year term (Art 62(2)).
Re-election: eligible any number of times (Art 57). In the USA a person can be elected President only twice. Only Rajendra Prasad has served two terms.

blocks.text: see Impeachment & vacancy for who acts when the office is vacant (Vice-President; Chief Justice M. Hidayatullah in 1969)

blocks.text: see Veto, ordinance & pardon for Zail Singh's pocket veto

items: MLCs and nominated members never vote for President; nominated MPs DO vote for Vice-President and DO take part in impeachment.
MLAs vote for President but do not take part in impeachment.
MLA vote value differs by State; every MP (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha) has the same value.
Population base is the 1971 census (frozen until the first census after 2026).

President: 50 proposers, 50 seconders and ₹15,000 deposit. Vice-President: 20 proposers, 20 seconders and ₹15,000 deposit. The deposit is lost if the candidate gets less than one-sixth of the votes polled.
Election disputes go to the Supreme Court only (Art 71). Acts done before the election is declared void stay valid. A vacancy in the electoral college is no ground to challenge the election.
Age 35; oath by Chief Justice of India; resignation to Vice-President; re-election unlimited (Art 57).
Quick numbers: term 5 years; impeachment notice 14 days; vacancy election 6 months; civil suit notice 2 months; ordinance lapses 6 weeks after Parliament reassembles.

subcards.title: Impeachment & vacancy (Art 56, 61, 62, 65)
subcards.summary: How the President can be removed, and who acts when the post is empty.
at_a_glance: Art 61 gives the procedure for impeachment (removal by Parliament) of the President
'Violation of the Constitution' – and the Constitution does not explain what this means
Either House of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha)
The President gets 14 days' written notice; the charge is signed by at least one-fourth (¼) of the total members of the House that starts it
Two-thirds (2/3) of the TOTAL membership of the House (not just members present) – needed in each House separately
Quasi-judicial (works like a court): one House makes the charge, the other House investigates it
Election within 6 months (Art 62); the new President gets a full 5-year term
The Vice-President (Art 65); if the Vice-President's post is also empty – the Chief Justice of India

head: Article
What it says
rows: The term is 5 years. The President can resign by a signed letter to the Vice-President. The President can be removed by impeachment. The President stays in office until the successor takes charge.
Procedure for impeachment of the President
Time for holding election to fill a vacancy in the President's office
The Vice-President acts as President when the post is empty, or does the President's work when the President is absent or ill
Parliament can make a law for situations the Constitution does not cover. Under this, Parliament made the President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969.
blocks.note: Do not confuse: Art 72 is the pardoning power; Art 74 is the Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President; Art 75 is the appointment of the Prime Minister; Art 123 is the ordinance power; Art 143 is the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (President asking the Court for its opinion).

blocks.text: see President: election & office (Art 52–62) for term, re-election and resignation details

blocks.title: Ground
items: Only one ground: 'violation of the Constitution'.
The Constitution does NOT define what 'violation of the Constitution' means – Art 61 only gives the procedure.
Criminal offence, moral wrong and unsound mind are NOT grounds – the Constitution does not mention them for impeachment.
The charge is brought by a House of Parliament – not by the CBI (Central Bureau of Investigation), CVC (Central Vigilance Commission), NIA (National Investigation Agency) or any court.

steps.detail: Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha can start it.

steps.step: 2. Signed by one-fourth (¼) of the members
steps.detail: At least one-fourth of the total members of the House that frames the charges must sign.
The resolution cannot be moved before this notice.
It needs a majority of two-thirds (2/3) of the TOTAL membership of that House – not just two-thirds of those present.
The President has the right to appear and to be represented (e.g. by a lawyer) at this investigation.

steps.step: 6. Other House also passes it by two-thirds (2/3) of its total membership
steps.detail: It must sustain (accept) the charges.
From the date the second House passes the resolution. No further order is needed.

items: It is called quasi-judicial (works like a court): one House acts as the accuser, the other House acts as the judge.
No President has been impeached so far (as of Nov 2026).

sections.heading: Who takes part: election vs impeachment

blocks.title: Same President, two different 'forums'
head: Group
Election (Art 54)
Impeachment (Art 61)
rows: Elected members of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
Elected MLAs (members of Legislative Assemblies) of States, Delhi and Puducherry

items: Nominated MPs (members chosen by the President, not elected) take part in impeachment but do NOT vote in the election.

MLAs vote in the election but do NOT take part in impeachment. So if asked 'part of the electoral college (the group that elects) but not of impeachment', the answer is 'State Legislative Assemblies'.

sections.heading: President vs judge vs Vice-President: how each is removed

blocks.title: Three removal methods
head: Aspect
President (Art 61)
Judge of Supreme Court or High Court (Art 124(4); Art 217 for High Court)
Vice-President (Art 67(b))
rows: 'Removal' – the Constitution does not use the word 'impeachment' for judges, but people commonly call it that
Removal – there is no formal impeachment
14 days' notice; ¼ members of the House sign
The motion is signed by 100 Lok Sabha members or 50 Rajya Sabha members (Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 – Laxmikanth calls it the Judges Enquiry Act)
The other House investigates; the President may appear and be represented
A 3-member committee: the Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court judge, a Chief Justice of a High Court, and a distinguished jurist (an eminent legal expert)
Two-thirds (2/3) of the total membership, in each House
Special majority in each House: a majority of the total membership AND two-thirds (2/3) of the members present and voting
Rajya Sabha passes it by effective majority (a majority of all its members at that time, leaving out vacant seats); then Lok Sabha agrees to it by a simple majority
Removed on passing in the second House
Both Houses send an address (formal request) to the President; then the President's order removes the judge
No judge has been removed so far. The motion against Justice V. Ramaswami (1991–93) failed in the Lok Sabha.

blocks.title: Other offices (for match-the-following)
items: Speaker of Lok Sabha: removed by a resolution passed by an effective majority of the Lok Sabha alone, after 14 days' notice.
Governor: there is no impeachment; the Governor holds office 'during the pleasure of the President' (the President can remove the Governor at any time).
Chief Minister: holds office 'during the pleasure of the Governor'.

blocks.text: see Vice-President (Art 63–71) for VP removal details

blocks.title: Five ways the post can fall vacant
head: Cause
Rule
Who acts meanwhile
rows: The election must be completed BEFORE the term ends. If it is delayed, the outgoing President continues until the successor takes charge. This prevents an 'interregnum' (a gap with no head of state).
The outgoing President himself – the Vice-President does NOT act
Resignation (by a letter to the Vice-President)
Election within 6 months of the vacancy (Art 62)
Death in office (Zakir Husain died in 1969 and Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed died in 1977 while President)
Any other reason – for example, the President is disqualified or the election is declared void (cancelled by the Supreme Court)
blocks.note: The newly elected President gets a FULL 5-year term from the day he takes charge – not just the remaining part of the old term.

blocks.title: Who acts as President
items: When the post is empty: the Vice-President acts as President until a new President is elected – at most 6 months (Art 65).
Temporary absence or illness (office not vacant): the Vice-President only discharges the functions until the President resumes.
While acting as President, the Vice-President does not work as Chairman of Rajya Sabha – the Deputy Chairman does that work.

If the Vice-President's post is also empty: the Chief Justice of India acts as President. If the Chief Justice's post is also empty, the senior-most available Supreme Court judge acts. This rule comes from the President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969, made by Parliament under Art 70.
The Speaker of Lok Sabha and the Prime Minister are NOT in this line.
Whoever acts as President gets all the powers and immunities (legal protections) of the President, and the salary and allowances fixed by Parliament.

blocks.title: Vacancy rule: President vs Vice-President
head: Aspect
President
Vice-President
rows: 'As soon as possible' (no fixed time limit)

items.what: President Dr. Zakir Husain dies in office
items.detail: Vice-President V.V. Giri becomes acting President.

items.what: Parliament makes the President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969 under Art 70
items.detail: It says: if both the President's and the Vice-President's posts are empty, the Chief Justice of India acts as President; if the Chief Justice's post is also empty, the senior-most available Supreme Court judge acts.

items.what: V.V. Giri resigns as Vice-President to contest the presidential election
items.detail: Now both offices are empty at the same time.

items.what: Chief Justice of India M. Hidayatullah acts as President under this Act
items.detail: He is the first (and so far only) Chief Justice to act as President.

items.what: M. Hidayatullah is elected Vice-President (unopposed – no one contested against him)
items.detail: So one person held three posts: Chief Justice of India, acting President and Vice-President.

items: The impeachment Article is Art 61 (not Art 56, 63 or 71). Art 56 is the term; Art 62 is the election to fill a vacancy; Art 65 is the Vice-President acting as President.
Signatures: one-fourth (¼) of members, not one-third (⅓). Notice: 14 days, not 30 days.
Majority: two-thirds (2/3) of the TOTAL membership – not two-thirds of members 'present and voting'.
'Violation of the Constitution' is NOT defined anywhere in the Constitution – Art 61(2) does not explain it.
Nominated MPs take part in impeachment; MLAs do not (but MLAs do vote in the election).
Term ends but no successor yet? The outgoing President continues – not the Vice-President, not the Chief Justice of India.
Both the President's and Vice-President's posts empty? The Chief Justice of India acts (as Hidayatullah did in 1969) – not the Speaker, the Prime Minister or the Attorney General.
The President sends the resignation to the Vice-President; the Vice-President sends it to the President.

subcards.title: Powers of the President
subcards.summary: What the President can do: executive, legislative, money, courts, defence, emergencies.
at_a_glance: Given to the President by Article 53
Executive, legislative, financial, judicial, diplomatic, military and emergency powers
The President, Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha (Article 79)
12 members with special knowledge of literature, science, art or social service
Only the Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha is permanent and is never dissolved
National Emergency – Art 352; President's Rule in a state – Art 356 (and Art 365); Financial Emergency – Art 360

blocks.text: The President is a constitutional authority (the office is created by the Constitution itself). He/she is the constitutional (formal, in-name) head of the Union executive. The real power is used on the advice of the council of ministers headed by the Prime Minister. (See the card 'Constitutional position'.)

blocks.title: Article 53 – executive power of the Union
head: Clause
What it says
rows: Executive power of the Union is vested in the President. He/she exercises it directly or through officers subordinate to him/her, in accordance with the Constitution.
Supreme command of the defence forces is vested in the President; its exercise is regulated by law.
Nothing in Art 53 transfers to the President any functions that an existing law has given to a state government or any other authority.
Nothing in Art 53 prevents Parliament from giving functions, by making a law, to authorities other than the President.
blocks.note: Executive power is vested in the President – NOT in the PM, the council of ministers or the 'Union Government'. Art 73: Union executive power extends to (a) all matters on which Parliament can make laws, and (b) rights and powers that India holds under treaties and agreements. But in a state, on matters where the state legislature can also make laws, it does not extend unless the Constitution or a law of Parliament expressly says so.

blocks.title: Articles often matched in exams
head: Article
Content
rows: Separation of the judiciary from the executive (a Directive Principle of State Policy, DPSP)
Executive power of the Union vested in the President
Constitution of Parliament (the President and the two Houses)
Summoning the Houses, proroguing them (ending a session) and dissolving the Lok Sabha
President's assent to bills passed by Parliament
Annual financial statement (commonly called the Budget)
Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (the President can ask the Supreme Court for its opinion)
State bills reserved by Governor for President's consideration

blocks.title: President vs Governor
head: Aspect
President
Governor
rows: No – Governor has none of these

blocks.title: Executive powers
items: All executive actions of the Government of India are formally taken in his/her name.

Makes rules on how orders issued in his/her name are authenticated (officially signed and certified). Also makes rules for the smooth running of government business and for dividing that work among ministers.
Appoints the Prime Minister and other ministers. They hold office 'during his/her pleasure' (as long as the President wishes; in practice, as long as they keep Lok Sabha's confidence).
Appoints the Attorney General (the Government of India's chief law officer), fixes his/her pay, and the Attorney General holds office as long as the President wishes.

Appoints the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners, the chairman and members of UPSC, state Governors, the chairman and members of the Finance Commission, and others.
Can ask the Prime Minister for information about the running of the Union government and about proposed laws.
If a single minister has decided a matter without the full council of ministers discussing it, the President can ask the PM to put that matter before the council.
Can appoint a commission to study backward classes, and can set up an Inter-State Council (to improve Centre–state and state–state coordination).
Directly governs Union Territories through administrators that he/she appoints.
Can declare any area a 'Scheduled Area' (a tribal-majority area given special protection); has powers over scheduled and tribal areas.

blocks.text: The President makes these appointments formally, but follows the procedures the Constitution lays down and acts on the advice of ministers. They are not his/her personal choice.
How the President chooses a PM when no party has a majority in Lok Sabha (a 'hung' House): see the card 'Constitutional position'

Art 79: Parliament consists of the President, the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) and the Lok Sabha (House of the People). The council of ministers and the PM are NOT part of this definition. The President is not a member of either House (Art 59) and does not sit in Parliament. Yet he/she is an integral (essential) part of it, because a bill passed by both Houses becomes an Act (law) only after the President gives assent (approval).

blocks.title: Legislative powers
head: Power
Detail
rows: Summon and prorogue (call and end sessions)

Summons each House 'at such time and place as he/she thinks fit'. The only rule: the gap between two sessions must not be more than 6 months. Holding three sessions a year is only a convention (practice), not a rule of the Constitution. No minimum number of sitting days in a year is fixed.
Dissolves the Lok Sabha – for example, when a government falls and no other government can be formed, so fresh elections are held. Rajya Sabha is a permanent House and is never dissolved.

When the two Houses disagree on an ordinary bill (one House rejects it, they disagree on amendments, or 6 months pass without the other House passing it), the President 'may' call a joint sitting of both Houses. The Speaker of Lok Sabha presides. Not available for money bills or Constitution amendment bills. The text of Art 108 does not say what happens if no joint sitting is called. Laxmikanth explains: the bill then ends and becomes dead, because a bill needs both Houses to pass it (Art 107).

Gives a special address to both Houses sitting together at the start of the first session after each general election and the first session of each year (Art 87). Can also address either House or both Houses together at any time, and send messages to the Houses (Art 86).
If both the Speaker and Deputy Speaker posts are vacant, appoints any Lok Sabha member to preside (chair the House). Same for Rajya Sabha if both the Chairman and Deputy Chairman posts are vacant.

Nominates 12 members to Rajya Sabha who have special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art and social service. (Earlier, the President could also nominate 2 Anglo-Indians to Lok Sabha; this was ended by the 104th Amendment Act, 2019.)

Decides whether an MP is disqualified (for example, for holding an 'office of profit' – a paid government post). He/she must first get the Election Commission's opinion and must act according to that opinion; this decision is final (Art 103). (Disqualification for defection under the Tenth Schedule is decided by the Speaker or Chairman, not the President.)
Prior recommendation (President's approval needed before a bill is introduced)

Needed before introducing: (1) a money bill; (2) a bill that involves spending from the Consolidated Fund of India; (3) a bill to form a new state or change state boundaries; (4) a bill on a tax in which states are interested; (5) a bill changing the meaning of 'agricultural income'; (6) a bill on the principles of distributing money to states; (7) a bill imposing a surcharge for the Centre's purposes. Also, a state bill that restricts freedom of trade needs his/her previous sanction (approval in advance).

On a bill passed by Parliament, the President can: give assent, withhold (refuse) assent, or return it for reconsideration. A money bill cannot be returned. If Parliament passes the returned bill again, he/she must give assent.

On a state bill that the Governor has reserved (sent) for the President, the President can: give assent, withhold assent, or direct the Governor to return it to the state legislature (not a money bill). Even if the state legislature passes it again, the President is not bound to give assent.

Issues ordinances (temporary laws) when both Houses, or either House, of Parliament are not in session and immediate action is needed. An ordinance must be approved by Parliament within 6 weeks after it meets again; otherwise it stops working.

Causes the reports of the CAG, UPSC, Finance Commission, National Commission for Scheduled Castes and others to be laid before Parliament. (The Public Accounts Committee report is not among these – that committee presents its own report to Parliament.)

Makes regulations (laws) for the Union Territories of Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, and Ladakh. For Puducherry, only when its assembly is suspended or dissolved.

blocks.text: Art 255: suppose a law needed the President's prior recommendation or previous sanction, and this was not taken. If the President later gave assent to that law, the law is not invalid for that reason. (Same rule when the Governor's recommendation was needed and the Governor or President gave assent.) So courts cannot strike down the law on that ground alone – the Constitution treats these requirements as 'matters of procedure only'.
Types of veto, conditions for ordinances, and related cases: see the card 'Veto, ordinance and pardon'

blocks.title: Financial powers
head: Power
Detail
rows: Introduced in Parliament only with his/her prior recommendation.

Causes the 'annual financial statement' to be laid before both Houses. This is a statement of the estimated income (receipts) and spending (expenditure) of the Government of India for the year. The Constitution does not use the word 'budget'.
No demand for grants (a request to Parliament to approve spending) can be made without his/her recommendation.
Can give advances (money in advance) from the Contingency Fund of India to meet unexpected expenditure.
Sets up the Finance Commission every five years to recommend how tax revenue should be shared between the Centre and the states.

blocks.text: These are NOT the President's functions: passing the Appropriation Bill or voting on demands for grants (Parliament does this); certifying that a bill is a money bill (the Speaker of Lok Sabha does this); auditing government accounts (the CAG does this).

blocks.title: Judicial powers
head: Power
Detail
rows: Appoints the Chief Justice of India and the judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts. He/she can remove them only after both Houses of Parliament pass an address (special resolution) asking for removal.
Can ask the Supreme Court for its opinion on any question of law or fact. The President is not bound to follow that opinion.

Can grant pardon (full release), reprieve (temporary stay of a sentence), respite (lesser sentence for special reasons), remission (shorter sentence), suspension, or commutation (a lighter type of punishment). This applies to court-martial (military court) cases, offences against Union laws, and all death sentences.

blocks.title: Diplomatic & military powers
head: Power
Detail
rows: Negotiated and concluded on behalf of the President, subject to Parliament's approval.
Represents India in international matters; sends Indian ambassadors and high commissioners abroad and receives those of other countries.
Supreme Commander of the defence forces (Art 53(2)); appoints the chiefs of the Army, Navy and Air Force. By practice, he/she takes the salute at the Republic Day parade as Supreme Commander.
Can declare war or make peace, subject to Parliament's approval. His/her command of the forces is regulated by law and is used on the advice of ministers.

blocks.title: Three emergencies
head: Type
Article
Ground
rows: War, external aggression or armed rebellion. Can be declared only after the Union Cabinet's decision is sent to him/her in writing (44th Amendment Act, 1978).
The government of a state cannot be carried on as per the Constitution (failure of constitutional machinery, Art 356); or a state does not follow the Union's directions (Art 365).
The financial stability or credit of India is threatened. The President can then order cuts in salaries, including those of Supreme Court and High Court judges.

blocks.text: Effects, approval periods and cases: see the card 'Emergency Provisions'

items: Executive power is vested in the President (Art 53), not the PM or council of ministers.
Art 53(3)(b): Parliament may, by making a law, give functions to authorities other than the President.
Parliament consists of the President and the two Houses (Art 79). The President is a part of Parliament but not a member of either House.
President dissolves Lok Sabha only; Rajya Sabha is never dissolved.
The President can summon Parliament at any place he/she thinks fit. The only rule is that the gap between two sessions must not be more than 6 months.
The 12 members nominated to Rajya Sabha must have knowledge of literature, science, art or social service. Sports, eloquence (speaking skill) and law are NOT in this list.
MP disqualification: President decides, but must act on the Election Commission's opinion.

President does not 'pass' bills (the two Houses pass them), does not conduct elections (the Election Commission does), and does not chair UPSC or the Civil Services Board. The Cabinet Secretary chairs the Civil Services Board at the Centre (in a state, the Chief Secretary chairs the state's Board) – not the PM.

subcards.title: Veto, ordinance & pardon
subcards.summary: How the President stops bills, makes temporary laws, and forgives punishments.
at_a_glance: Absolute, suspensive and pocket veto. NOT qualified veto
Pardon a death sentence, and give clemency for court-martial (military court) sentences
No fixed time limit. Supreme Court opinion on the Presidential Reference, 20 Nov 2025

head: Article
What it says
rows: There shall be a President of India
Procedure for impeachment of the President
President's power to pardon, reprieve, respite, remit, suspend or commute
Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President
Appointment of PM and other ministers
PM's duty to give information to the President
President's assent to bills passed by Parliament
President can ask the Supreme Court for advice (advisory jurisdiction)
Governor's assent to bills passed by the State legislature
Bills reserved by the Governor for the President's consideration
If the required prior sanction or recommendation was not taken, the Act is still valid if assent is later given

blocks.text: Art 52–62 in detail → see President: election & office
A bill passed by both Houses of Parliament becomes an Act only after the President's assent (Art 111). Lok Sabha alone or Rajya Sabha alone is not enough.

blocks.title: President's three choices on a bill (Art 111)
items: Give assent
Withhold assent. The bill ends and does not become an Act
Return it to Parliament for reconsideration (not allowed for a Money Bill). If Parliament passes it again, with or without changes, the President MUST give assent

blocks.title: Why a veto? (two aims)
items: Stop hasty, ill-considered laws
Stop laws that may be unconstitutional

blocks.title: Four types of veto in the world
head: Veto
Meaning
India's President?
rows: The President refuses assent (withholds it); the bill ends
The President returns the bill; Parliament can overrule him by passing it again with an ORDINARY majority
The President takes no action at all; the bill stays pending for an unlimited time
The legislature can overrule the veto only by a HIGHER (special) majority
No — the US President has it

blocks.title: Which veto applies to which bill
head: Bill
Union (Parliament)
State bill reserved for President
rows: Give assent, withhold assent, or return for reconsideration
Give assent, withhold assent, or direct the Governor to return it to the State legislature
Give assent or withhold assent. Cannot return it
Give assent or withhold assent. Cannot return it
Must give assent (24th Amendment, 1971). No veto at all
Cannot be introduced in a State legislature

blocks.title: Veto used in practice
head: Year
President
Veto
Bill
rows: PEPSU Appropriation Bill. Parliament passed it during President's Rule in PEPSU (Patiala and East Punjab States Union), but President's Rule was revoked before the bill reached the President

Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, which put restrictions on press freedom. He kept it pending. In 1989 the next President, R. Venkataraman, returned it for reconsideration, and the new National Front Government dropped it
Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament (Amendment) Bill. Parliament passed it without the President's prior recommendation, which was required

blocks.title: Key points
items: Absolute veto is usually used in two cases: (a) private members' bills (bills moved by an MP who is not a minister); (b) government bills, when the cabinet resigns after the bill is passed but before assent, and the new cabinet advises the President not to sign
A Money Bill is normally given assent, because it is introduced in Parliament only with the President's prior permission

Pocket veto is possible because the Constitution sets NO time limit for the President to decide. The US President must return a bill within 10 days. So it is said that 'the Indian President's pocket is bigger' than the American President's
Art 255: an Act does not become invalid just because the required prior sanction or recommendation was not taken, if the President later gave assent
The veto works as a check and balance between the President and Parliament. But the President uses it on the advice of the Council of Ministers, not on his own

blocks.text: Art 74 aid and advice → see Constitutional position

sections.heading: State bills reserved for the President (Art 200, 201)

steps.detail: Goes to the Governor
Four choices: give assent, withhold assent, return to the legislature (not a Money Bill), or reserve the bill for the President
Three choices: give assent, withhold assent, or direct the Governor to return it to the legislature (not a Money Bill)
If the legislature passes it again, it goes back to the President, who is NOT bound to give assent

items: Once reserved, the decision is the President's, not the Governor's
The State legislature cannot overrule the President. So if the President withholds assent even after the bill is passed again, that is an ABSOLUTE veto
Art 201 sets no time limit, so the President can use a pocket veto on reserved State bills too
The President cannot reserve a State bill on his own; only the Governor reserves it
The Constitution expressly says that in some matters the Governor acts in his own discretion (Art 163)

Concurrent List subject: if a State law is reserved and gets the President's assent, it prevails over the earlier Union law in that State (Art 254(2)). Parliament can later override it by passing a new law on the same subject
Sarkaria Commission recommended: when the President withholds assent to a State bill, the reasons should be told to the State Government

blocks.text: Governor's powers in full → see Governor

items.what: Supreme Court judgment, State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu (bench of 2 judges: J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan)
items.detail: Fixed time limits: Governor 1 to 3 months, President 3 months. Using Art 142 (Supreme Court's power to do complete justice), it declared 10 Tamil Nadu bills 'deemed assented' (treated as if assent was given)

items.what: President Droupadi Murmu makes a Reference under Art 143
items.detail: She asked the Supreme Court 14 questions on the powers under Art 200 and Art 201

items.what: 5-judge Constitution Bench opinion (CJI B.R. Gavai, Surya Kant, Vikram Nath, P.S. Narasimha, A.S. Chandurkar)
items.detail: All judges agreed. Questions 12 and 14 were not answered, as they were not relevant

blocks.title: What the Court said (Nov 2025)
head: Question
Answer
rows: Can courts fix time limits for the Governor or the President?
Is a bill 'deemed assented' (treated as approved) if the time limit passes?
No — that would be the judiciary taking over executive functions
Can the Supreme Court use Art 142 to take the decision in their place?
Only three: give assent, reserve for the President, or withhold assent and return the bill to the Assembly. He cannot simply withhold and sit on it
Can the Governor reserve a bill that the Assembly has passed again?
Yes. The Governor may assent or reserve it for the President (this changed the April 2025 view that he must assent)
Can courts examine these decisions (are they justiciable)?

Not on merits (courts cannot judge whether the decision is right). But if there is long, unexplained, endless delay, a court may issue a limited mandamus (court order to perform a duty) asking him to decide within a reasonable time
Must the President take the Supreme Court's opinion on every reserved bill?
Can a court examine a bill before it becomes law?
blocks.note: An Art 143 opinion is advisory (advice to the President). No later change found as of Nov 2026.

blocks.text: Art 123 lets the President make temporary laws (ordinances) during the recess of Parliament. While in force, an ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament. It is called his most important legislative power.

blocks.title: Four limits on an ordinance
head: Limit
What it means
rows: Only when both Houses, or either one House, is not in session. An ordinance made while both Houses are in session is void. It is not a parallel power to make laws alongside Parliament

The President must be satisfied that circumstances need immediate action. This satisfaction can be challenged in court for mala fides (bad faith) (Cooper case, 1970). The 38th Amendment (1975) made his satisfaction final and beyond court review; the 44th Amendment (1978) removed that protection
Only on subjects on which Parliament can make laws. It has the same limits as an Act of Parliament, so it cannot take away or reduce Fundamental Rights

It ends (lapses) 6 weeks after Parliament reassembles; if the two Houses meet on different dates, count from the later date. It ends earlier if both Houses pass resolutions disapproving it. If Parliament approves it, it continues as an Act

blocks.title: Can / cannot
items: Maximum life: 6 months and 6 weeks. (6 months is the longest gap allowed between two sessions; 6 weeks is the time after reassembly)
Can be retrospective (can take effect from a back date)
Can amend or repeal any Act of Parliament or another ordinance, including a tax law
CANNOT amend the Constitution
Can be withdrawn by the President at any time
Not a discretionary power. The President makes or withdraws an ordinance only on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister
Has nothing to do with a National Emergency (Art 352); no war or armed rebellion is needed
The President needs nobody's instructions to make an ordinance. A Governor needs the President's instructions in 3 cases (Art 213)
This power is unusual: the US and UK Constitutions do not have it. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar justified it as needed to deal with sudden situations
Under Lok Sabha rules, a bill that replaces an ordinance must come with a statement explaining why the ordinance was needed
2002: President A.P.J. Abdul Kalam returned the ordinance on electoral reforms to the Cabinet. The Cabinet sent it back without any change, and he then signed it under Art 123

blocks.title: Ordinance cases
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Cooper case (1970) (R.C. Cooper v. Union of India)
The President's satisfaction can be questioned in court on the ground of mala fides (bad faith)
An ordinance can be examined by courts (judicial review)

Between 1967 and 1981 the Bihar Governor issued 256 ordinances and kept them alive for 1 to 14 years by issuing them again and again. The Court said such repeated re-issue (re-promulgation) is a 'fraud on the Constitution'
An ordinance cannot be used as a substitute for law made by the legislature
Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017) (7 judges)
Re-issuing ordinances again and again is a fraud on the Constitution. Placing (laying) the ordinance before the legislature is compulsory. The executive's satisfaction can be reviewed by courts
Confirmed and strengthened the D.C. Wadhwa ruling

blocks.text: Governor's ordinance (Art 213) → see Governor

blocks.title: Art 72 — President can pardon a convict where the sentence is
items: For an offence against a Union law
By a court martial (military court)
A sentence of death

blocks.text: This power is independent of the courts; the President does not act as a court of appeal. It has two aims: to correct mistakes made by courts, and to give relief from a sentence that is too harsh.

blocks.title: Five forms of clemency
head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: Removes both the sentence and the conviction. The person is freed from all punishments and disqualifications
Replaces punishment with a lighter form
Death sentence changed to rigorous imprisonment; rigorous imprisonment changed to simple imprisonment
Reduces the length of the sentence without changing its type
2 years of rigorous imprisonment reduced to 1 year of rigorous imprisonment
Gives a lesser sentence in place of the original one because of a special fact
The convict is pregnant or physically disabled
Stops the carrying out of a sentence (especially death) for a time
Gives the convict time to ask for pardon or commutation

blocks.title: President (Art 72) vs Governor (Art 161)
head: Aspect
President — Art 72
Governor — Art 161
rows: Offences against State laws (matters to which the State's executive power extends)
Yes. Only the President can pardon a death sentence, even when the death sentence is under a State law
Death sentence: suspend, remit or commute
Yes. The Governor shares this power with the President
All five (for offences against State laws)

blocks.title: Pardon cases
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: The President uses the power on the advice of the Union Cabinet. Courts can review it only in a limited way
It is not the President's personal power

(1) The convict has no right to an oral hearing. (2) The President may examine the evidence again and take a different view from the court. (3) He acts on Cabinet advice. (4) The Supreme Court need not lay down guidelines for using the power. (5) Courts can review a decision only if it is irrelevant, irrational, mala fide (in bad faith) or discriminatory
Laid down the main principles on the pardoning power
Epuru Sudhakar v. Govt. of A.P. (2006)
The Court cancelled a remission given by the Andhra Pradesh Governor. A clemency decision can be reviewed if it is mala fide (in bad faith) or based on irrelevant or outside considerations
Showed limited judicial review in actual use

items: India's President has absolute, suspensive and pocket veto. He has NO qualified veto (the US President has it)
A Money Bill cannot be returned. A Constitution Amendment Bill must be given assent (24th Amendment, 1971)
Union bill passed again by Parliament: the President must give assent. Reserved State bill passed again by the State legislature: the President is NOT bound
Pocket veto example: President Zail Singh, 1986, Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill
The Constitution sets no time limit for assent. Supreme Court (Nov 2025): courts cannot fix one, and there is no 'deemed assent'

An ordinance can be made even when one House is in session, but never when both Houses are in session. It cannot amend the Constitution or reduce Fundamental Rights. It can be retrospective. It is not discretionary
Ordinance life: 6 weeks from the reassembly of Parliament; maximum 6 months and 6 weeks
Only the President can give clemency for court-martial sentences and pardon a death sentence. But a Governor CAN commute or remit a death sentence

subcards.title: Constitutional position of the President
subcards.summary: President is the formal head; the Council of Ministers really runs the government.
at_a_glance: Nominal (de jure, 'in law') executive. The real (de facto, 'in fact') executive is the Council of Ministers led by the Prime Minister
Art 53, Art 74, Art 75; also Art 77, Art 78, Art 88
42nd Amendment, 1976 made the ministers' advice binding on the President
44th Amendment, 1978: President can send advice back once; the advice given after reconsideration is binding
No discretion written in the Constitution; only 'situational' discretion when a situation leaves room for judgement
Same position as the King under the English Constitution
Persuasive (he can advise and warn), not coercive (he cannot force)
First citizen of India; a constitutional authority (office created by the Constitution)

blocks.text: India has a parliamentary system. So the President is only the formal (nominal) head. The real power lies with the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister (PM). The President acts on their 'aid and advice' (help and advice).

blocks.title: Two executives
head: Aspect
President
PM and Council of Ministers
rows: Nominal (in name only), de jure (in law) or titular executive
Real or de facto (in fact) executive
Elected indirectly by an electoral college (elected MPs and MLAs), not by the people directly
President appoints the PM (Art 75); other ministers are appointed on the PM's advice
Not responsible to the Lok Sabha; can be removed only by impeachment
Collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Art 75(3)) — the whole Council falls if it loses the Lok Sabha's confidence

blocks.title: Same pattern in the States
head: Office
Role
rows: Head of Union Council of Ministers; Council collectively responsible to Lok Sabha (Art 75(3))
Head of State Council of Ministers; Council collectively responsible to the State Legislative Assembly (Art 164(2))

blocks.title: Labels examiners use
items: First citizen of India; symbol of the unity, integrity and solidarity of the nation.
A constitutional authority (the office is created by the Constitution itself, Art 52) — not a statutory authority (created by an Act of Parliament).
The constitutional head of the Union executive is the President — not the Prime Minister.
His influence is persuasive (he can advise, encourage and warn), not coercive (he cannot force the government) and not merely ceremonial.
Art 52 to Art 78 (Part V, Chapter I) deal with the Union Executive.

blocks.title: Ambedkar's description (Constituent Assembly)
head: Ambedkar said
Meaning
rows: Same position as the King under the English Constitution
Our model is copied from Britain, not from the USA
Head of the State but not of the Executive
He is the formal head only; the ministers run the executive
Represents the nation but does not rule the nation
He is a symbol of the nation, not its ruler
A ceremonial device or a seal
The nation's decisions are announced through him, like a seal on a document
Can do nothing against the ministers' advice, and nothing without their advice
He is bound by the ministers' advice
Cannot dismiss ministers while they have a majority (unlike US President)
Ministers stay in office as long as they have the Lok Sabha's support

head: Article
What it says
rows: The executive power of the Union is vested in (formally given to) the President. He uses it directly or through officers under him, as the Constitution says
There is a Council of Ministers with the PM at its head to aid and advise the President. He 'shall' (must) act on that advice. He may ask them once to reconsider it
No court can inquire whether any advice was given by the ministers, and if given, what that advice was
The President appoints the PM; other ministers are appointed on the PM's advice
Total number of ministers, including the PM, cannot exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha (added by 91st Amendment, 2003)
Ministers hold office 'during the pleasure of the President' (he can remove them, in practice on the PM's advice) — this is individual responsibility
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha — this is the foundation of the parliamentary system
The President gives the oaths of office and secrecy to ministers, including the PM
A person who is not a member of Parliament can be a minister for at most 6 consecutive months; he must become a member within that time
All executive action of the Government of India is formally taken in the name of the President
Orders signed (authenticated) as per the President's rules cannot be challenged in court on the ground that the President did not personally make them
The President makes rules for the smooth working (transaction) of Government business and for dividing that work among ministers
Duties of the PM towards the President (see the steps below)
Ministers may speak in both Houses, in a joint sitting and in Parliament's committees, but can vote only in the House they are a member of

blocks.title: Art 78 — the PM is the link between the President and the Council of Ministers

steps.detail: The PM must tell the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers on running the Union, and all proposals for new laws
The PM must give any information on administration and proposed laws that the President asks for
If the President asks, the PM must place before the whole Council a matter that one minister decided alone without the Council considering it

blocks.title: PM's role that follows from these
items: The PM recommends persons for appointment as ministers. Among the PM's powers usually listed, this is the only one written in the Constitution (Art 75(1)). Allocating portfolios (departments), transferring ministers and calling Cabinet meetings come from conventions (practice) and rules, not the Constitution.
The PM advises the President on summoning (calling) and proroguing (ending a session of) Parliament.
The PM is the Chairman of NITI Aayog (the government's policy think-tank).
Executive power is NOT vested in the PM (it is in the President, Art 53). The Civil Services Board is chaired by the Cabinet Secretary, not the PM.

blocks.text: see Powers of the President

head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: For the first time, made the President bound to act on the ministers' advice
The President may send the advice back once for reconsideration; the advice given after reconsideration is binding
Anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule) — not about the President; a common wrong option
Size of the Council of Ministers limited to 15% of the Lok Sabha strength
blocks.note: Today, the relationship between the President and the Council of Ministers is governed by the 44th Amendment.

items.what: President K.R. Narayanan sent back the Cabinet's advice to impose President's Rule in Uttar Pradesh
items.detail: The Cabinet dropped the proposal; the Kalyan Singh government survived

items.what: Narayanan sent back the Cabinet's advice to impose President's Rule in Bihar
items.detail: The Cabinet gave the same advice again; President's Rule was imposed in February 1999

items.what: President A.P.J. Abdul Kalam sent back the electoral-reforms ordinance (Art 123 — President's power to make ordinances) for reconsideration
items.detail: The Cabinet sent it back unchanged on 24 August 2002, and he signed it the same day — the Representation of the People (Amendment) Ordinance, 2002

blocks.text: If the President refuses to act on binding advice, it is a violation of the Constitution, which is the ground for impeachment (Art 61). See: Impeachment & vacancy.
The Constitution gives the President no discretion (power to act on his own judgement), unlike a Governor. But some situations leave room for his own judgement. This is called situational discretion.

head: Situation
What the President does
rows: Hung Lok Sabha (no party or alliance has a clear majority), or the PM dies suddenly and there is no obvious successor
Appoints as PM the person most likely to win the Lok Sabha's confidence, and asks him to prove majority by a floor test (vote in the House)
The Council of Ministers cannot prove that it has the confidence of the Lok Sabha
May dismiss the Council of Ministers
The Council of Ministers has lost its majority and still advises dissolving the Lok Sabha
May either dissolve the Lok Sabha or refuse to dissolve it

blocks.title: Related limits
items: National Emergency (Art 352): the President can proclaim it only when the Union Cabinet's decision is given to him in writing (added by the 44th Amendment).

Disqualification of an MP (for example, for holding an office of profit) under Art 103: the President decides, but he must first get the Election Commission's opinion and must act according to that opinion.
Pardon (Art 72): the President uses it on the Union government's advice; courts can review it only to a limited extent. See: Veto, ordinance & pardon.
Supreme Commander of the defence forces: this power is used as regulated by law, and on ministers' advice like his other powers.

head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: The Council of Ministers continues even after the Lok Sabha is dissolved; Art 74 is mandatory (there must always be a Council)
The President can never act without a Council of Ministers
The President's 'satisfaction' in the Constitution means the satisfaction of the Council of Ministers, not his personal satisfaction
Confirms he is a formal head who acts on aid and advice
S.P. Anand v H.D. Deve Gowda (decided 1996; AIR 1997)
Upheld H.D. Deve Gowda's appointment: a person who is not a member of either House can be appointed PM, but must become a member within six months (Art 75(5) applies to the PM too)
The PM is under the same 6-month rule as other ministers
S.R. Chaudhuri v State of Punjab (2001)
A non-member minister who fails to get elected within six months cannot be re-appointed minister during the same Assembly term without getting elected (Art 164(4); same logic for Art 75(5))
Stops the misuse of giving repeated 6-month appointments to non-members
Devi Lal oath case (K.M. Sharma v Devi Lal, 1990)
Calling Devi Lal 'Deputy PM' in his oath was only a description; the oath was valid
A Deputy PM is just a minister and gets no extra powers

blocks.title: Art 361 — President and Governors
head: Immunity
Detail
rows: The President (or Governor) cannot be questioned by any court for using the powers and duties of the office
No criminal case can be started or continued against him during his term
No court can order his arrest or imprisonment during his term
A civil case about his personal acts can be filed during his term, but only after giving 2 months' written notice — it is not permanently barred
This immunity does NOT stop proper cases against the Government of India or a State government

blocks.title: No legal responsibility of ministers for the President's acts
items: In Britain, every order of the King is countersigned (signed again) by a minister, and that minister is legally responsible for it.
In India, the President's order does not need a minister's countersignature; and courts cannot ask what advice was given (Art 74(2)).

sections.heading: Compare: Indian President vs British Monarch vs US President

head: Aspect
Indian President
British Monarch
US President
rows: Parliamentary system with a constitutional monarchy
Elected indirectly by elected MPs and elected MLAs (including Delhi and Puducherry)
Elected indirectly through the Electoral College, which is chosen by the people's votes
Real head of State and Government
5 years; can be re-elected any number of times
4 years; cannot be elected more than twice (22nd Amendment of US Constitution)
Yes (Art 74, as changed by the 42nd and 44th Amendments); he may send advice back once
Yes, by convention (established practice), not by written law
No — his ministers (called 'secretaries') are only his advisers
Taken from Parliament; collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha
Taken from Parliament; responsible to the House of Commons
Not members of Congress (US Parliament); responsible only to the President
Can dismiss them at will (whenever he wants)
Yes, on the advice of the PM
Yes, on the advice of the PM
By impeachment for violation of the Constitution
No impeachment; holds office for life (can abdicate)
Impeachment charges by the House of Representatives; trial by the Senate
Countersignature by a minister and legal responsibility
Not needed; ministers have no legal responsibility for his acts
Every order countersigned by a minister; rule that 'the King can do no wrong' (the minister is responsible)
Persuasive: he has the right to be consulted, to encourage and to warn
As Bagehot wrote: the right to be consulted, to encourage and to warn
Coercive: he directs the administration himself

items: 42nd Amendment (1976) = advice made binding for the first time. 44th Amendment (1978) = President can send it back once, then it is binding. The present position is under the 44th Amendment.
Executive power is vested in the President (Art 53), not the PM. All government action is taken in the President's name (Art 77).
Art 74 = Council of Ministers to aid and advise; Art 75 = appointment of the PM; Art 78 = PM's duty to inform the President; Art 88 = ministers can speak in both Houses.
The President has only situational discretion, not constitutional discretion.
Influence = persuasive. Title = first citizen of India; a constitutional authority.
Courts cannot ask what advice was given (Art 74(2)). In India, no minister's countersignature is needed on the President's orders.
The Council of Ministers continues even after the Lok Sabha is dissolved (U.N.R. Rao case, 1971).
The Council of Ministers is limited to 15% of the Lok Sabha (91st Amendment, 2003) — not 20%. The President gives the oaths to the PM and the ministers.

subcards.title: Vice-President (Art 63–71)
subcards.summary: Who the Vice-President is, how chosen and removed, and what he does.
at_a_glance: Art 63–71, Part V of the Constitution (Chapter I – The Executive)
Second highest office; next to the President in the Table of Precedence
All members of both Houses of Parliament – elected AND nominated members. State MLAs do NOT vote
5 years from the day he enters office; can be re-elected any number of times
The President (or a person the President appoints)

Only by a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by effective majority (majority of all its current members), which the Lok Sabha must agree to by simple majority; 14 days' notice needed; this is NOT impeachment
Chairman of the Rajya Sabha automatically because he is VP (Art 64); acts as President when needed (Art 65)
C.P. Radhakrishnan – 15th VP, sworn in 12 Sept 2025 (as of Nov 2026)

blocks.title: Articles on the Vice-President (Part V)
head: Article
What it says
rows: There shall be a Vice-President of India
VP is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Council of States)
VP acts as President when the President's post is vacant, or does the President's work when the President is absent or ill
Election of the Vice-President (who votes, qualifications)
Term of office (5 years), resignation, removal
When to hold the election to fill a vacancy; term of the person so elected
Oath or affirmation by the VP
How the President's work is done in situations not covered by the Constitution – Parliament makes a law for this
Disputes about the election of the President or the VP – decided by the Supreme Court
blocks.note: 'Ex-officio' means holding a post automatically because of another post. The VP is Chairman of the Rajya Sabha simply because he is VP; no separate election is needed.

items: The office is modelled on the American Vice-President.

In the Table of Precedence (order of rank on ceremonial occasions): 1 President, 2 Vice-President, 3 Prime Minister, 4 Governors (within their own States), 5 Former Presidents, 5A Deputy Prime Minister, 6 Chief Justice of India and Speaker of Lok Sabha (both share rank 6). So the order is VP, then PM, then Governor, then Speaker.

Some scholars call him 'His Superfluous Highness' (meaning: a high office with little work), because the Constitution gives the VP very few real powers of his own. The office exists to keep political continuity – someone is always ready to step in if the President's post falls vacant.
It is an indirect election – the people do not vote; Members of Parliament (MPs) vote.
Electoral college (the group of people who vote in this election) = ALL members of BOTH Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha), including NOMINATED members.
Members of State Legislative Assemblies (MLAs) and of State Legislative Councils (MLCs) take NO part.

Method: proportional representation by single transferable vote (each voter ranks the candidates as 1, 2, 3… in order of preference); voting is by secret ballot. This is the same method as the President's election.
In the original Constitution, the two Houses met together in a joint meeting to elect the VP. The 11th Amendment Act, 1961 replaced this joint meeting with an electoral college.

Nomination: the candidate needs at least 20 electors (MPs) as proposers and 20 more as seconders, and must deposit ₹15,000 as security in the Reserve Bank of India (rule from the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, as amended in 1997).
Election disputes: they are inquired into and decided ONLY by the Supreme Court, and its decision is final (Art 71).
The election cannot be challenged on the ground that the electoral college was incomplete (that is, some seats in Parliament were vacant at the time of voting) – Art 71(4).
If the Supreme Court declares the VP's election void (cancelled), the acts he did as VP before that declaration still remain VALID.

blocks.title: President vs Vice-President: election
head: Aspect
President
Vice-President
rows: Elected MLAs (including those of Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir)
Different for MLAs and MPs (worked out by a formula)
Each MP has one equal vote
Proportional representation by single transferable vote, secret ballot

blocks.text: Why do MLAs not vote for the VP? Dr. B.R. Ambedkar explained: the President is head of the State and his powers cover both the Centre and the States, so MLAs must have a say in choosing him. The VP's normal job is only to preside over the Rajya Sabha; he acts as President only rarely and for a short time, so MLAs need not vote.
See also: President – election and office (value of votes, list of Presidents)

blocks.title: Qualifications (Art 66)
head: Must be
Note
rows: Qualified for election to the RAJYA SABHA
NOT the Lok Sabha – being qualified for the Lok Sabha is the rule for the President
Not holding any office of profit

No office of profit (a paid government post) under the Union, a State, a local authority or any public authority. But a sitting President, VP, Governor, or Union or State minister is NOT treated as holding an office of profit, so such a person can contest.

blocks.title: Oath (Art 69)
items: Taken before the President, or a person the President appoints for this.
He swears to: (1) bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution; (2) faithfully discharge the duties of his office.
Compare: the President's oath is taken before the Chief Justice of India (CJI).

blocks.title: Conditions of office
items: He must not be a member of either House of Parliament or of a State legislature. If an MP, MLA or MLC is elected VP, his seat is treated as vacated on the date he ENTERS the VP's office (the same rule applies to the President).
He must not hold any other office of profit (paid government post).

blocks.title: Term (Art 67)
items: 5 years from the date he enters office.
Even after 5 years, he continues in office until his successor takes charge.
He can be re-elected any number of times (for example, Dr. S. Radhakrishnan got a second term).

blocks.title: Removal of the VP (Art 67) – not impeachment

steps.detail: No resolution can be moved without at least 14 days' notice

steps.step: Resolution moved ONLY in the Rajya Sabha
steps.detail: Cannot start in the Lok Sabha

steps.step: Rajya Sabha passes it by effective majority
steps.detail: Effective majority = majority of all the then members of the Rajya Sabha (total strength minus vacant seats)

steps.step: Lok Sabha agrees by simple majority
steps.detail: Simple majority = majority of members present and voting
The Constitution does not mention any ground (reason) for removal

blocks.title: How removal differs (common match question)
head: Office
How removed
rows: Impeachment for 'violation of the Constitution'; needs 2/3 of the total membership of each House
Rajya Sabha resolution by effective majority, which the Lok Sabha agrees to; no ground stated
Resolution by effective majority of Lok Sabha alone
Address (formal request to the President) by both Houses with special majority, for proved misbehaviour or incapacity
Holds office during the pleasure of the President
Holds office during the pleasure of the Governor

blocks.title: Vacancy
items: A vacancy can arise by: end of the 5-year term, resignation, removal, death (Krishan Kant was the first VP to die in office, 2002), or otherwise (for example, disqualification, or the election being declared void).
At the end of the term: the election to fill the post must be held BEFORE the term ends.
After resignation, death or removal: the election is held 'as soon as possible' – there is NO fixed time limit, unlike the 6-month limit for filling the President's post.
The newly elected VP gets a FULL fresh 5-year term (not the predecessor's remaining term).
The Constitution has NO post of 'acting Vice-President'. While the VP's post is vacant, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha does the Chairman's work in the House.
Example: Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned on 21 July 2025 for health reasons, by a letter to the President; the election to fill the post was held on 9 Sept 2025 (as of Nov 2026).

sections.heading: Functions: Rajya Sabha Chairman and acting President

blocks.title: 1. Ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Art 64)
head: Point
Fact
rows: Similar to those of the Lok Sabha Speaker
How he differs from the Speaker
He cannot decide whether a bill is a Money Bill, and he does not preside over a joint sitting of both Houses – both these are powers of the Lok Sabha Speaker
Is he a member of the House?
No – the Chairman is NOT a member of the Rajya Sabha (Speaker is a member of Lok Sabha)
Cannot vote in the first instance (in normal voting); votes only when votes are equally divided – this is called a casting vote
When a resolution to remove him as VP is being considered
He cannot preside over the House; he may be present, speak and take part in the proceedings, but cannot vote
When can he be removed as Chairman?
Only when he is removed from the office of Vice-President

blocks.title: 2. Acts as President (Art 65)
items: When the President's office is vacant (death, resignation, removal or otherwise): the VP acts as President for at most 6 months, and within that time a new President must be elected. He acts only until the new President takes charge.
When the President is absent, ill or otherwise unable to work (but the office is NOT vacant): the VP does the President's work until the President resumes his duties.
While acting as President, the VP does NOT do the Chairman's work; the Deputy Chairman does it.

Examples: V.V. Giri (1969, after President Zakir Husain died) and B.D. Jatti (1977, after President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed died) acted as President. Dr. S. Radhakrishnan did the President's work in June 1960 (when President Rajendra Prasad was on a tour of the USSR) and in July 1961 (when Rajendra Prasad was ill).
The VP has no independent everyday executive role of his own; he does not run the government alongside the PM.

blocks.title: Emoluments
items: The Constitution fixes NO salary for the VP as VP. He gets his salary as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

The Chairman's salary was raised from ₹1.25 lakh to ₹4 lakh per month by the Finance Act 2018 (effective from 1 Jan 2016). It is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (paid without a vote of Parliament).
Pension of a retired VP: 50% of his salary (under the Vice-President's Pension (Amendment) Act, 2008; earlier it was ₹20,000 per month).
While acting as President, he gets the President's salary and allowances, not the Chairman's.

blocks.text: See also: Impeachment and vacancy (who acts as President when both the President's and VP's posts are vacant – the Chief Justice of India, as in 1969)

blocks.title: Indian VP vs US VP
head: Aspect
India
USA
rows: Ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
President of the Senate (presides over it)
Only ACTS as President until a new President is elected (at most 6 months)
BECOMES President for the rest of the predecessor's term
Elected together with the President on a joint ticket (through the Electoral College)
blocks.note: India's office is modelled on the US office, but the key difference is succession: the US VP becomes President, the Indian VP only acts as President for a short time.

blocks.title: Vice-Presidents of India
head: No.
Vice-President
Term
Remember
rows: First VP; two terms, both won unopposed (1952, 1957); later President
Acted as President in 1969; later President
Won unopposed; earlier, as Chief Justice of India, he acted as President in 1969 when both the President's and VP's posts were vacant
First VP to die in office
Elected 9 Sept 2025 (452 votes against 300 for B. Sudershan Reddy); oath given by President Droupadi Murmu (as of Nov 2026)

items: VP elections won unopposed (no rival candidate): 1952, 1957, 1979, 1987.
VPs who served two terms: S. Radhakrishnan and Hamid Ansari.
VPs who later became President: S. Radhakrishnan, Zakir Husain, V.V. Giri, R. Venkataraman, S.D. Sharma, K.R. Narayanan.
Never VP: Gulzarilal Nanda (was acting PM only); Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed and N. Sanjiva Reddy (were President directly, never VP).
Nominated MPs vote for VP but NOT for President; MLAs vote for President but NOT for VP.
VP must be qualified for RAJYA SABHA (not Lok Sabha).
VP's oath: before the PRESIDENT (President's oath: before the CJI).
VP resigns to the President; President resigns to the VP.
Removal resolution starts ONLY in the Rajya Sabha; it is NOT impeachment; no ground is stated; 14 days' notice is needed.
The VP acts as President for at most 6 months; he does not get the rest of the President's term (the US VP does).
There is no 'acting VP' in the Constitution; a VP vacancy is filled 'as soon as possible'; the new VP gets a full 5-year term.
No salary as VP – he is paid as Rajya Sabha Chairman. He has only a casting vote (used when votes are tied). The 11th Amendment, 1961 created the electoral college for the VP.
